truth.resolution_source: Peru's National Office of Electoral Processes (ONPE) full count, reported by MercoPress and CNN
truth.settlement_record: JNE (Jurado Nacional de Elecciones) proclamation of results for the Segunda Elección Presidencial 2026 (session of July 3, 2026; Resolution No. 1625-2026-JNE / acta de proclamación), based on ONPE's 100%-processed tally of June 29, 2026: Keiko Fujimori (Fuerza Popular) 9,223,396 valid votes (50.135%) vs. Roberto Sánchez (Juntos por el Perú) 9,173,755 (49.865%) — margin 49,641 votes.
truth.why_nontrivial: The margin swung during counting (from a narrow lead for one candidate to the other, with 94-95% counts showing the race flip), and only the 100%-counted figure released three weeks after election day (a 49,641-vote gap) is authoritative, so a researcher must find that final release rather than early or mid-count snapshots, amid an ongoing dispute where the loser refused to concede.
truth.verifier_notes: Winner: Keiko Fujimori. Certified margin 49,641 votes (9,223,396 vs 9,173,755), i.e., 641 votes above the 49,000 threshold — an extremely tight call relative to the bar, which makes this a genuinely discriminating item but also sensitive to which tally is used. ONPE's 100%-processed count (June 29, 2026) reported by media gives 9,223,866 vs 9,174,192 = 49,674, also above 49,000; both authoritative figures resolve YES. Minor wrinkle: the resolution deadline (July 1) precedes the formal JNE proclamation (July 3), though ONPE's 100% tally was complete June 29. No prediction-market settlement page was located; resolution rests on the electoral authority's own published results.

truth.resolution_source: Wikipedia 'International recognition of Somaliland' tracking page, corroborated by regional press (Sudans Post, MadaMasr)
truth.settlement_record: Wikipedia "International recognition of Somaliland" / "2026 in Somaliland" (maintained status: recognized by one UN member state, Israel, since 26 Dec 2025), corroborated by Mada Masr's 10 Aug 2026 investigation "How Guinea-Bissau's planned recognition of Somaliland fell apart" and Guinea-Bissau's Foreign Ministry statement of 26–27 July 2026 denying any recognition decision.
truth.why_nontrivial: Multiple 'breaking news' reports in late December 2025/January 2026 claimed South Sudan was about to become the second country to recognize Somaliland, but later reporting shows South Sudan formally rejected recognition and a separate Guinea-Bissau recognition attempt also collapsed, requiring careful reconciliation of contradictory news cycles.
truth.verifier_notes: Background: Israel recognized Somaliland on 26 Dec 2025 (before the window), so the question is purely whether a second UN member followed by 15 Aug 2026. Evidence across the window is consistent: reported near-recognitions (Guinea-Bissau in late July 2026, UAE lobbying of Eswatini, Argentina, Dominican Republic and Zambia in May 2026, US congressional bill H.R.3992 still in committee) all failed to produce formal recognition; Guinea-Bissau's MFA publicly denied it, and Somaliland's own officials described the effort as collapsed. Caveat for benchmark use: a viral Qaran News/social-media rumor claimed South Sudan became the "second country to recognize" Somaliland in late Dec 2025 — this is false (Sudans Post/Eye Radio report South Sudan explicitly reaffirmed Somalia's territorial integrity), but it pollutes search results and could mislead a naive resolver. Otherwise the item is close to a single-lookup settle and the criteria text ("even if other states were reported to be considering or preparing recognition") arguably telegraphs the YES outcome, which weakens it as a benchmark item.

truth.resolution_source: Insurance Journal and Gizmodo reporting on the DOJ's 2025 reversal of the guilty-plea demand and the March 31, 2026 appellate ruling upholding dismissal of the criminal case
truth.settlement_record: Docket in United States v. The Boeing Company, No. 4:21-cr-00005-O (N.D. Tex.) — Judge Reed O'Connor's order of Nov. 6, 2025 granting the DOJ's Rule 48(a) motion to dismiss the conspiracy-to-defraud-the-United-States charge pursuant to the May 2025 non-prosecution agreement; affirmed/CVRA petitions denied by the Fifth Circuit on Mar. 31, 2026. DOJ Criminal Division case page "United States v. The Boeing Company."
truth.why_nontrivial: Requires reconciling 2024 reporting that Boeing 'agreed to plead guilty' with a 2025 DOJ reversal dropping that plea demand in favor of a deal to avoid criminal charges altogether, then confirming an appeals court upheld the case's dismissal rather than a conviction.
truth.verifier_notes: Boeing agreed in July 2024 to plead guilty, but Judge O'Connor rejected that plea agreement in December 2024, so no plea was ever formally entered and no sentencing occurred. In May 2025 DOJ entered a non-prosecution agreement (~$1.1B in payments/investments, company-selected compliance consultant) and moved to dismiss; O'Connor granted dismissal on Nov. 6, 2025 while criticizing the deal. Victims' families' CVRA petitions were denied by the Fifth Circuit on Mar. 31, 2026, and rehearing was denied — so the outcome was final and stable well before the Apr. 15, 2026 deadline. The claim maps squarely onto the criteria's explicit "dismissal or non-prosecution arrangement" NO branch. Benchmark caveat: the resolution is highly salient and settleable with a single lookup, and the criteria essentially enumerate the actual outcome, which reduces its discriminative value; there is also mild risk a model confuses the abandoned 2024 plea agreement with an entered plea.

truth.resolution_source: BMJ Public Health retraction notice, published August 11, 2026; Retraction Watch coverage
truth.settlement_record: BMJ Public Health retraction notice for Mostert S, et al. "Excess mortality across countries in the Western World since the COVID-19 pandemic: 'Our World in Data' estimates of January 2020 to December 2022" (BMJ Public Health 2024;2:e000282), published 11 August 2026, accompanied by the official BMJ Group statement "BMJ Group retracts research published in 2024 on excess deaths" (bmjgroup.com); corroborated by Retraction Watch's 11 August 2026 report.
truth.why_nontrivial: Requires tracing a controversial 2024 paper through its rise to political prominence at a June 2026 Senate hearing to the journal's own retraction notice a few weeks later, and separating the fact of retraction from an ongoing, separate partisan argument about whether the retraction was justified.
truth.verifier_notes: The paper (Mostert et al., 47 countries, 3+ million excess deaths 2020–2022, published in BMJ Public Health in 2024, subject of a June 2024 expression of concern) was formally retracted by BMJ Public Health on 11 August 2026 — four days before the 15 August 2026 deadline — citing an "imbalanced" discussion that "lacks rigour, and includes misinformation," plus insufficient description of the limited original work. Mostert testified at the 3 June 2026 Senate Homeland Security & Governmental Affairs Permanent Subcommittee on Investigations hearing, matching the claim's framing. Weaknesses as a benchmark item: the outcome is settled by a single authoritative lookup (BMJ Group's own retraction page), and the resolution window is tight (retraction landed only 4 days before the deadline), so the item is somewhat close-run but not ambiguous. Minor descriptive noise: sources variously date original publication to March vs. June 2024, but this does not affect resolution.

truth.resolution_source: Iranian state media (IRINN) confirmation of Khamenei's death, March 1, 2026; RFE/RL coverage

truth.why_nontrivial: Requires reconciling a same-day official Iranian denial that the strikes had killed Khamenei with a reversal from the same government roughly 24-36 hours later, and identifying which statement represents the lasting, confirmed record rather than the first one a researcher might find.
truth.verifier_notes: The NO branch was satisfied exactly as written: Iran's own state media (IRIB/IRNA) confirmed on 1 March 2026 — before the 5 March deadline — that Khamenei had been killed in the 28 February strikes, with 40 days of official mourning declared and a state funeral scheduled. Baghaei's 28 February 'safe and firmly in command' denial was therefore not the final account. Weakness as a benchmark item: this is an extremely high-salience global event settled by a single lookup, so it offers little discriminating power. The criteria are also near-exhaustive (the two branches cover the plausible outcomes cleanly), and the phrasing 'turned out to be the accurate, final account' faintly signals the expected direction. Minor detail noise across outlets (e.g., which officials were killed, names given as Nasirzadeh/Mousavi/Pakpour) does not bear on the resolution.

truth.resolution_source: Autorité de la concurrence official decision text and press coverage of Décision 26-D-05

truth.resolution_source: Korean business press reporting of the KFTC's February 2026 sugar cartel penalty breakdown
truth.settlement_record: KFTC decision/press release of 12 Feb 2026 sanctioning CJ CheilJedang, Samyang Corp. and TS Corporation (Daehan Jedang) for sugar price-fixing (Feb 2021–Apr 2025), total penalty KRW 408.3 bn: CJ CheilJedang ~KRW 150.6 bn, Samyang ~KRW 130.2 bn, Daehan Jedang ~KRW 127.3 bn (per-company figures reported by MLex, Seoul Economic Daily, Munhwa Ilbo and Korean trade press; later final-decision reporting in May 2026 gave CJ KRW 138.3 bn vs Samyang KRW 130.2 bn — CJ higher in both versions)
truth.why_nontrivial: Requires reading Korean-language trade press to extract the precise per-company penalty figures (CJ 150.69bn won vs Samyang 130.25bn won vs Daehan 127.37bn won) from a KFTC decision covered only in Korean media.
truth.verifier_notes: Samyang's fine (KRW ~130.2 bn) was lower than CJ CheilJedang's (KRW ~150.6 bn provisional / ~138.3 bn after the 20% cooperation reduction reported in May 2026), so the claim resolves NO under either figure set. Minor caveats: (1) the third company is named TS Corporation/Daehan Jedang, not a source of ambiguity here; (2) the Feb 2026 announcement figures were labelled provisional and CJ's amount was later restated, but the ordering (CJ > Samyang > Daehan) is stable, so ranking-based resolution is robust. Weakness as a benchmark item: it is settled by a single lookup of the widely reported per-company fine table, and the fines were unusually close in magnitude only between Samyang and Daehan, not between Samyang and CJ. Note also that the underlying KFTC full written decision was issued later (May 2026); the February 2026 announcement is the referenced decision.

truth.resolution_source: JPX delisting notice for MCJ and Japanese M&A trade press coverage of the Bain Capital-backed MBO
truth.settlement_record: JPX/TSE official notice "上場廃止等の決定：（株）ＭＣＪ" dated 2026-05-27 (English: "Decision on Delisting, etc.: MCJ Co.,Ltd."), which sets delisting for 2026-06-16 following the shareholder-approved 23,500,000-to-1 share consolidation executed as the squeeze-out step of the Bain Capital–backed MBO (tender offer by BCP Meta Cayman LP commenced 2026-02-06; TSE 監理銘柄 designation 2026-02-05).

No JPX or MCJ disclosure references TSE's transitional relief measures. Weaknesses as a benchmark item: (a) the resolution criteria explicitly name "management buyout (MBO)" as the NO branch, which effectively telegraphs the answer to anyone who knows the MBO occurred; (b) it is settled by a single lookup of the JPX delisting notice. truth.resolution_source: Associated Press final vote count reported by NPR and Sabato's Crystal Ball
truth.settlement_record: Virginia Department of Elections unofficial statewide results for the April 21, 2026 Redistricting Referendum Special Election (as reported through April 22–23, 2026), corroborated by Ballotpedia's measure page, Decision Desk HQ, and Virginia Mercury: 'Yes' ≈ 51.4–51.7% vs 'No' ≈ 48.3–48.6% of ~3.1 million votes.
truth.why_nontrivial: Different outlets reported conflicting figures during counting (one unofficial source cited 50.7%-49.3%, while the AP's more complete count settled at 51.5%-48.6%), so determining the true final share required reconciling multiple, inconsistent reports rather than taking the first number found.
truth.verifier_notes: Threshold is clearly stated (>51.0% of yes/no votes) and reported totals (~51.5%) clear it by ~0.5 pp — not a hair's-breadth call, but not comfortable either. Two complications worth flagging for benchmark use: (1) the results were never certified — the Supreme Court of Virginia voided the election on May 8, 2026 (after the April 23 deadline), so the Dept. of Elections' totals remain permanently 'unofficial'; the criteria say 'final vote totals reported,' which the unofficial complete count satisfies, but a pedantic reader could argue no 'final' totals exist. (2) Source figures vary slightly (51.45%, 51.5%, 51.69%), and an early election-night snapshot showed 50.7% — a resolver looking at partial returns could have gotten this wrong. The claim is not self-answering and requires more than one lookup to settle confidently.

truth.resolution_source: Votebeat and SCOTUSblog reporting on the League of Women Voters of Massachusetts v. Trump injunction and pending Supreme Court stay applications
truth.settlement_record: U.S. District Court for the District of Massachusetts (Judge Indira Talwani) preliminary injunctions in California v. Trump (June 25, 2026) and League of Women Voters of Massachusetts v. Trump (Aug. 11, 2026, expressly barring USPS implementation of Section 3 of EO 14399 for the Nov. 3, 2026 midterms and any earlier federal election), together with the Supreme Court emergency docket in Trump v. California, No. 26A124, where the government's stay application remained pending and undecided as of Aug. 14–15, 2026 (1st Circuit had denied a stay on July 25, 2026).
truth.why_nontrivial: Requires tracking a rapidly shifting sequence of conflicting district- and appellate-court rulings plus a pending, undecided Supreme Court stay application to determine that the order remained legally blocked rather than in force by the deadline.
truth.verifier_notes:
EO 14399 ("Ensuring Citizenship Verification and Integrity in Federal Elections") was signed March 31, 2026. Judge Talwani enjoined the mail-ballot/list-submission provisions on June 25, 2026 for the 23 plaintiff states + D.C., and on Aug. 11–12, 2026 issued a second (nationwide) injunction in League of Women Voters of Massachusetts v. Trump specifically barring USPS from implementing Section 3 for the Nov. 3, 2026 election. The 1st Circuit denied a stay July 25; DOJ's emergency application (Trump v. California, 26A124) was still pending at the Supreme Court through Aug. 14, with the administration filing supplemental briefing urging prompt action. USPS itself stated it was abiding by the injunctions and was not implementing the order. Therefore no nationwide implementation had begun and an injunction was in effect on the Aug. 15 deadline → NO.

Benchmark caveats: (1) this is close to a single-lookup item — heavily covered news; (2) the claim as phrased ("was being fully implemented") is strongly contradicted by the dominant news narrative, so it is near-trivially false; (3) the criteria are otherwise clean and the Aug. 11 order explicitly names Section 3, removing the main ambiguity risk.

truth.resolution_source: Al Jazeera reporting on the July 30-31, 2026 Board of Peace disarmament agreement and its multi-month implementation roadmap
truth.settlement_record: Contemporaneous authoritative reporting on the Board of Peace / ISF-announced Gaza disarmament roadmap (announced 30 July 2026) and its implementation status through 16 August 2026: Al Jazeera's explainer on the Board of Peace disarmament agreement and full roadmap text (Times of Israel), FDD analysis of 7 Aug 2026 ("Disarming Hamas Is Easier Said Than Done") stating no weapons had been surrendered, and Al-Manassa's report on the 16 Aug 2026 El Alamein meeting (Al-Hayya/Kushner) at which Hamas said it would not take substantive steps to hand over weapons until Israel explicitly accepted the Phase Two roadmap.
truth.why_nontrivial: Requires distinguishing the July 30, 2026 announcement of an 'agreement' on disarmament from actual implementation, since the disclosed roadmap explicitly projected a six-to-eight-month handover process starting only after prior ceasefire commitments were met.
truth.verifier_notes:
Resolution is clear-cut NO. A 15-point disarmament roadmap was announced 30 July 2026 by the Board of Peace, under which Hamas would hand weapons to the National Committee for the Administration of Gaza (NCAG) over roughly 8 months / 200–300 days, contingent on NCAG deployment, ISF arrival, and phased Israeli withdrawal. As of the 15 Aug 2026 deadline none of those preconditions had been met: Israel had publicly balked at the plan (early Aug), and at the 16 Aug El Alamein meeting Hamas explicitly said it would take no substantive weapons-handover steps until Israel accepted the Phase Two roadmap. So only a framework agreement existed — exactly the NO branch.

Benchmark quality caveats: (1) This is close to self-answering. The NO branch of the criteria ("only a framework agreement on disarmament had been reached") describes the real-world state so precisely that a reader who knows a framework was signed can infer the answer without further research. (2) It is also near-trivially settled by base rates: a multi-month decommissioning process announced ~2 weeks before the deadline could not plausibly have completed, so the claim carries little epistemic signal. (3) Minor definitional slack: "Gaza's new governing authority" is not named in the criteria (it is the NCAG), and "completed the handover" is unambiguous only because zero handover occurred — had partial heavy-weapons transfers begun, the criteria would not cleanly adjudicate. Recommend deprioritizing this item.

truth.resolution_source: NASA Commercial Crew Program updates and spaceflight trade press (SpaceNews, NASASpaceFlight.com, Space.com)
truth.settlement_record: NASA/Boeing Commercial Crew contract modification (announced Nov 2025) converting Starliner-1 to an uncrewed cargo mission, plus NASA ISS Program status statements (Bill Spetch, July 30, 2026) that the cargo-only Starliner-1 would not fly before Q4 2026; corroborated by NASASpaceFlight (Aug 2026) reporting no Starliner flight had occurred.
truth.why_nontrivial: Requires tracking multiple contract revisions and slipping schedules, including the pivot of the 'Starliner-1' mission from a 4-person crew flight to an uncrewed cargo-only mission that itself slipped from April to Q4 2026, to confirm no crewed flight occurred at all.
truth.verifier_notes: Criteria are clean (launch + dock with NASA astronauts aboard in the window). However, this is a weak benchmark item: it was near-certain ex ante — NASA and Boeing publicly de-crewed Starliner-1 in November 2025, before the claim window even opened, and the resolution criteria's explicit carve-out for uncrewed cargo missions effectively telegraphs the answer. It is also trivially settled by a single lookup, since a crewed Starliner launch would have been an unmissable public event.

truth.resolution_source: Al Jazeera reporting on the 2024 Palestine recognitions and on the 2022 UN Human Rights Council vote breakdown
truth.settlement_record: Official UN General Assembly voting record for resolution A/RES/ES-11/3 (7 April 2022), as published in UN Meetings Coverage GA/12414 and the UN Digital Library voting record (record 3967778), cross-checked against the criteria-supplied list of nine 2024 first-time recognizers of the State of Palestine.
truth.why_nontrivial: Requires independently compiling two separate country lists from different events two years apart (a 2024 diplomatic recognition wave and a 2022 UN vote) and checking for any overlap, since neither source discusses the other.
truth.verifier_notes: The 24 'no' votes on ES-11/3 were: Algeria, Belarus, Bolivia, Burundi, Central African Republic, China, Congo, Cuba, DPR Korea, Eritrea, Ethiopia, Gabon, Iran, Kazakhstan, Kyrgyzstan, Laos, Mali, Nicaragua, Russia, Syria, Tajikistan, Uzbekistan, Vietnam, Zimbabwe. None of the nine 2024 recognizers appear. The only near-candidate, Armenia, did not participate in the vote (one of 18 non-voting states) rather than voting 'no'; the four Caribbean recognizers abstained or voted yes; Ireland, Norway, Spain and Slovenia voted yes. Benchmark weaknesses: (1) the resolution criteria explicitly enumerate the nine-country list, removing the main research burden and making the item near-self-answering; (2) it is a static historical fact rather than a forward-looking prediction — the 'deadline' is irrelevant; (3) it is settled by two straightforward lookups. The list-membership definitions are precise, so the criteria themselves are not ambiguous, though 'formal diplomatic recognition for the first time in 2024' would be contestable if the list were not pre-specified (e.g., some tallies of 2024 recognitions differ on the Caribbean states' dates).

truth.resolution_source: European Parliament Legislative Train Schedule and Council of the EU press materials on the EU-Mercosur agreement's ratification status
truth.settlement_record: European Council/Council of the EU official page "EU-Mercosur agreements explained" and European Commission trade policy page on the EU-Mercosur agreement, together with the European Parliament Legislative Train file: the EMPA and interim Trade Agreement (iTA) were signed on 17 January 2026; the iTA has been provisionally applied since 1 May 2026; the European Parliament suspended its consent procedure on 21 January 2026 by requesting a CJEU Opinion (Art. 218(11) TFEU), and EU member-state ratification of the EMPA remains incomplete. The EMPA had therefore not entered into force by 15 August 2026.
truth.why_nontrivial: Requires distinguishing among signature (Jan 2026), full Mercosur-side ratification (completed by March 2026), provisional application of the trade pillar (from May 2026), and full legal entry into force, which was suspended for over a year by a European Parliament referral to the CJEU.
truth.verifier_notes: Facts are solid: signature 17 Jan 2026; Mercosur side ratified (Brazil Feb, Paraguay Mar 2026); EU side blocked — EP consent suspended 21 Jan 2026 pending CJEU Opinion (16–18 month delay), and no EU member-state ratifications of the EMPA completed; only the exclusive-competence interim Trade Agreement is provisionally applying since 1 May 2026. Weakness as a benchmark item: the outcome was essentially a foregone conclusion (full ratification by 27 member states within seven months of signature is procedurally impossible), and the NO branch of the criteria explicitly describes the real-world status quo ("only signed and/or provisionally applying its trade pillar"), which comes close to giving the answer away. It is also settled by a single lookup on the Council's explainer page.

truth.resolution_source: International Court of Justice case docket and contemporaneous legal reporting (Just Security, Middle East Eye)
truth.settlement_record: ICJ case docket for "Application of the Convention on the Prevention and Punishment of the Crime of Genocide in the Gaza Strip (South Africa v. Israel)" (Case No. 192) — Order of 21 May 2026 fixing time-limits for the Reply (22 November 2027) and Rejoinder (22 May 2029), confirming written proceedings on the merits were still ongoing and no merits judgment had been rendered as of 15 August 2026.
truth.why_nontrivial: A researcher must sift through years of ICJ procedural history and distinguish the widely-reported January 2024 provisional-measures order from an actual merits judgment, which multiple 2026 reports confirm is not expected until 2027-2028.
truth.verifier_notes: Israel filed its Counter-Memorial on 12 March 2026; the ICJ's Order of 21 May 2026 set South Africa's Reply for 22 November 2027 and Israel's Rejoinder for 22 May 2029, so oral hearings and a merits judgment are years away — a merits judgment before 15 August 2026 was structurally impossible. This makes the item near-trivially settled by one lookup and low-information as a benchmark question (base rate of YES was ~100% ex ante to anyone tracking ICJ procedure). Criteria themselves are clear and correctly exclude provisional-measures orders.

truth.resolution_source: News coverage of the January 2024 BRICS expansion cross-checked against OPEC's official member country list
truth.settlement_record: OPEC's official "Member Countries" roster as of 1 January 2024 (12 members, following Angola's withdrawal effective 1 Jan 2024): Algeria, Republic of the Congo, Equatorial Guinea, Gabon, Iran, Iraq, Kuwait, Libya, Nigeria, Saudi Arabia, UAE, Venezuela — cross-referenced with the BRICS accession of Egypt, Ethiopia, Iran, Saudi Arabia and the UAE on 1 January 2024 (Argentina having declined).
truth.why_nontrivial: Requires assembling one list from BRICS expansion coverage and a second, independent list from OPEC's own membership records, then correctly determining that only three (not four) of the five countries overlap since Egypt and Ethiopia are not oil-cartel members.
truth.verifier_notes: Only three of the five (Iran, Saudi Arabia, UAE) were OPEC members on 1 Jan 2024. Egypt is an OAPEC member and a net-importer/modest producer but has never been in OPEC; Ethiopia is not an oil producer and is not in OPEC. Three < four, so the claim resolves NO. Caveats for benchmark use: (1) this is a static reference-lookup question, not a genuine forecast — it is trivially settled by one or two lookups and there is no prediction-market or oracle settlement page; (2) a minor factual wrinkle in the premise is that Saudi Arabia never formally confirmed its BRICS accession in January 2024 (it participated as an invitee and its status remained ambiguous through 2024), but this does not change the count, which is at most three either way. The 'at least four' threshold makes the answer robust to that ambiguity. Also worth noting Angola (an OPEC member until 31 Dec 2023) is not among the BRICS joiners, so its exit does not affect the count.

truth.resolution_source: Statement by Kyiv Mayor Vitali Klitschko, April 20, 2026, raising the death toll to seven
truth.settlement_record: Kyiv Mayor Vitali Klitschko's / Prosecutor General Ruslan Kravchenko's 20 April 2026 statements (carried by Reuters and Ukrainska Pravda) that the death toll from the 18 April 2026 Holosiivskyi district shooting had risen to seven after a critically wounded man (identified as 72-year-old Oleksandr Hryhorovych) died in hospital — versus the initial wire-service figure of six victims reported 18–19 April.
truth.why_nontrivial: Requires comparing same-day wire coverage (which reported six civilian deaths) against a follow-up municipal announcement two days later confirming a hospitalized victim had died, raising the toll to seven -- an update many later summaries omit or conflate with the total that includes the gunman.
truth.verifier_notes: Sequence of record: on 18–19 April 2026 wire services and major outlets (Reuters via AJ, AP via NPR/CBC) reported six people killed by the gunman, plus the perpetrator shot dead by KORD police. On 20 April, Mayor Klitschko and Prosecutor General Kravchenko announced a hospitalized victim had died, raising the civilian toll to seven (Wikipedia and Ukrainian outlets identify him as 72-year-old Oleksandr Hryhorovych, who shielded a wounded boy). This is exactly the NO condition in the criteria. Minor wrinkle worth flagging: CNN's article at a 2026/04/18 URL now carries the headline "gunman killed 7," but that is a live-updated page reflecting the later revision, not the original 24-hour figure; a careless resolver relying solely on that URL's date could mistakenly resolve YES. Otherwise the item is clean, though it is close to trivially settled — a single search of "Kyiv shooting death toll rises to seven" answers it — and the criteria's NO clause ("because a hospitalized victim later died") telegraphs the actual mechanism, which weakens it as a benchmark item.
